content.title: About
content.content: A hamburger is a hot sandwich consisting of a beef patty placed between a split bun, often accompanied by cheese, lettuce, tomato, onion, sauces and seasonings. In school cafeterias of 1698 it was prepared from simple, locally available ingredients and served as a hearty meal for students.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first school hamburger appeared in 1698 in a historic school cafeteria, where it was prepared by student‑cooks.
The traditional bun was lightly toasted over an open fire, and the patty was cooked on a cast‑iron griddle.
The original recipe used only pure beef, without any soy or plant‑based fillers.
Hamburgers were often served with sauerkraut instead of modern sauces.
In some schools, melted cottage cheese was used in place of cheese, as it was more readily available.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: The beef patty provides high‑quality protein essential for growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Source of iron
items.content: Beef contains heme iron, which is more readily absorbed than plant‑based iron.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: Hamburgers supply B12, B6 and niacin, supporting nervous system function and metabolism.

items.title: Energy dense
items.content: The combination of protein, fat and carbohydrates in the bun offers sustained satiety and quick energy.

items.title: Provides fiber
items.content: When topped with lettuce, tomato and onion, the sandwich adds dietary fiber beneficial for digestion.

items.title: High in saturated fat
items.content: The patty and cheese can contain significant saturated fat, which may increase cardiovascular risk if consumed frequently.

items.title: Salt and additives
items.content: Historical recipes often relied on salt and dried spices for flavor, which can be problematic for people with hypertension.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: The wheat bun contains gluten, posing a risk for individuals with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Foodborne illness risk
items.content: Undercooked beef may harbor pathogenic bacteria, so the patty should be cooked thoroughly.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Hamburgers are typically eaten with the hands, holding the bun. They can be topped with mustard, ketchup or a homemade sauce. Optional additions include fresh lettuce, tomato slices, onion, and a slice of cheese that melts over the hot patty.

content.title: Storage
content.content: A freshly prepared hamburger is best consumed immediately. For storage, separate the components: keep the cooked patty refrigerated for up to 2 days, the bun in a dry paper bag, and the vegetables in an airtight container. Reheat the patty thoroughly before assembling.
